reconcile.connective: Henry locates the one exception to Qohelet's "nothing new" in the gospel's new creation and heaven's promised newness (2 Cor 5:17; Rev 21:5).

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible catalogues this as a direct clash: Qohelet's flat "nothing new" against five NT promises that God makes things new.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/new.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: If we would be entertained with new things, we must acquaint ourselves with the things of God, get a new nature; then old things pass away, and all things become new, Co2 5:17. The gospel puts a new song into our mouths. In heaven all is new (Rev 21:5), all new at first, wholly unlike the present state of things, a new world indeed (Luk 20:35), and all new to eternity, always fresh, always flourishing.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry directly reconciles Eccl 1:9's 'nothing new' with 2 Cor 5:17 and Rev 21:5 by carving out the gospel's/heaven's new creation as the singular exception to the 'under the sun' cycle Qohelet describes.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry's own comment on Ecclesiastes 1:9-10 treats this exact tension directly, naming 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Revelation 21:5 as the one exception to 'nothing new'; John Haley's Alleged Discrepancies (1874) was checked (full-text search of the archive.org djvu.txt) and does not treat this verse pairing, so the row's own harmonizing commentator is used instead.

link.title: Is there a Bible contradiction in Ecclesiastes 1:9-10?
link.note: Distinguishes Solomon's claim about human satisfaction 'under the sun' from God's distinct new-creation promises elsewhere in scripture.
